headline: Appledore Ledges Give Up Cod to 6 Pounds While the Piscataqua Runs Thick with Stripers
subhead: Thirteen miles of coastline is plenty when you know the bottom — groundfish holding tight to the Shoals structure while the river does the striper work.
body_markdown:
People hear thirteen miles of New Hampshire coast and figure there's nothing to write about. I've been running my 20-foot Lund out to the Shoals before sunup for going on fifteen years and I still haven't fished all of it. Thirteen miles on the chart doesn't mean thirteen miles of water — it means the Piscataqua pouring out past Portsmouth Harbor, Gosport Harbor tucked in behind Appledore and Star, and enough broken ledge and cobble bottom around the Shoals to keep a small boat guy busy every single trip. I fish it like it's a hundred and thirty miles. That's the whole secret.

This week the groundfish bite off Appledore held up better than the Hampton stuff, which tells you where I spent my mornings. Cod to six pounds came off the northeast side of the island in 60 to 80 feet, jigging diamond jigs tipped with a strip of mackerel belly on the slack before the tide turned, then switching to bait — whole clams and chunked mackerel on a two-hook bottom rig — once the current picked up and the jigs stopped hanging straight down. Haddock are around but they're not stacked the way they were in June. I marked pods on the sounder over some of the rockier patches south of Star Island and picked at them for maybe four or five keepers a trip, nothing you'd call a slam dunk. If you want haddock right now you need to be willing to move around and burn some gas checking marks instead of anchoring on one pile and hoping.

Water out at the Shoals is still running in that classic low-60s range at depth, which is exactly why the groundfish are behaving normally while everything south of the Merrimack is chasing peanut bunker blitzes in warm water. We don't get that show up here in mid-August and I wouldn't want it — cold, clean water holding cod and haddock on structure is the New Hampshire pattern, and it's held true again this week. We flagged this a week back — said this zone would trail the warmer water to the south and keep its own rhythm through the transition, and that's exactly what's playing out. No albies, no bonito, no blitzing bass chasing bunker schools on the surface. Just steady, honest groundfish and river stripers doing what they do this time of year.

Speaking of the river — the Piscataqua has been the better bet for stripers all week, and it's the current that makes it, not the moon phase alone. We came off the new moon on the 12th and the tidal flow built exactly like I expected, and the bite at current-driven structure sharpened right up with it. I've been working the seams below the Route 1 bridge and down around the General Sullivan area on the last two hours of the incoming, drifting live mackerel and eels on a three-way rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in that push. Fish from 26 to 34 inches, a handful over the 28-to-31 slot going back, but enough keepers in that window to make it worth the trip. The back eddies on the Portsmouth side, right where the current breaks off the pilings, have been holding fish tucked up tight — a slow-trolled bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig through there on the last of the ebb has worked when the straight drift didn't.

Hampton Harbor has been more up and down. The inlet by Great Boars Head fishes well on the push of the incoming, especially the first two hours after dead low when bait gets funneled through the channel, but I've had mornings there with almost nothing showing and mornings with a dozen schoolies to 24 inches on soft plastics — five-inch white paddletails on a half-ounce jighead, worked slow along the bottom edge of the channel drop. Seabrook side of the harbor has snapper blues thick in the back creeks, which is normal for mid-August and a decent sign that adult blues will keep building through the fall as those fish grow into it. If you've got kids who want bent rods, that's your spot — small Kastmasters or Gotcha plugs off the docks near the bridge.

Mackerel are still around the Shoals in good numbers, which is half the reason the cod fishing has held — bait's there and the structure holds it. I jig for mackerel on light tackle first thing to fill the bait bucket, then switch over to the groundfish gear once I've got what I need. It's an efficient way to fish a small boat out there and it costs you nothing but twenty minutes.

Flounder have been an afterthought this year in the harbors — a few keepers on sandworms and clam bellies in Rye Harbor on calm mornings, but nothing to plan a trip around.

Looking ahead, I don't expect much to change through the coming week. The tide's still building off that new moon push, so I'd keep working the Piscataqua current seams on the incoming for stripers and stick with the Appledore ledges for cod on the slack-into-building tide. If the wind stays out of the southwest and keeps things calm, I'll be back at the Shoals before most people's coffee is done brewing. That's still the way to fish this coast — early, small, and smart about the water you've got instead of wishing for more of it.
